definitions.plain: The luck of finding something good while you were looking for something else.
definitions.poetic: Fortune's habit of leaving gifts on paths you never meant to walk.
definitions.riddle: Hunt one treasure and I slip a better one into your pocket, unasked.

etymology: Coined by Horace Walpole in 1754, after a Persian tale of three princes who kept stumbling on discoveries they had not sought.
usage: By pure ___, the missing letter turned up inside a borrowed book.

definitions.plain: A strong longing to travel and see far places.
definitions.poetic: The itch that packs a bag before the mind has agreed to go.
definitions.riddle: I am a hunger no kitchen can feed; only a horizon quiets me, and never for long.

etymology: Borrowed whole from German — roaming joined to longing — in the first years of the twentieth century.
usage: Her ___ flared with every train whistle that crossed the valley.

definitions.plain: A bittersweet longing for times gone by.
definitions.poetic: Yesterday, lit gold by the lamp of missing it.
definitions.riddle: The farther you sail from a shore, the sweeter I make it look.

etymology: Greek for the ache of the homeward road — coined in 1688 as a medical diagnosis for Swiss soldiers pining in foreign camps.
usage: The smell of woodsmoke filled him with ___ for his grandfather’s cabin.

definitions.plain: A sudden moment of understanding that changes everything.
definitions.poetic: Lightning indoors: one flash, and the whole room of the mind is lit.
definitions.riddle: I arrive uninvited in bathtubs and on staircases, and after me nothing looks the same.

etymology: From the Greek for ‘a showing forth’, once reserved for divine appearances and a feast on the sixth of January.
usage: Halfway through washing the dishes she had an ___ about the unfinished poem.

definitions.plain: A gentle, lingering sadness with no single cause.
definitions.poetic: Rain that falls inside a person while the sky stays dry.
definitions.riddle: Too soft to be grief, too heavy to be rest — I am the blue hour of the heart.

etymology: From the Greek for black bile, one of the four humours once thought to govern the temper.
usage: A pleasant ___ settled on the porch as the last light left the garden.

definitions.plain: The state of being alone, especially by choice and at peace.
definitions.poetic: Aloneness worn as a warm coat rather than a wound.
definitions.riddle: Crowds destroy me, and yet I am no enemy of the ones you love.

etymology: From the Latin for ‘alone’, the same root that gave the language ‘sole’ and ‘desolate’.
usage: He kept Sunday mornings for ___, tea, and the slow crossword.

definitions.plain: Playful, fanciful humor; a taste for odd and charming notions.
definitions.poetic: The soap-bubble logic by which a teapot might well be a house for wrens.
definitions.riddle: I turn umbrellas into rowboats and errands into expeditions, and I weigh nothing at all.

etymology: A softened form of a seventeenth-century nonsense word for a fanciful trifle, cousin to ‘flim-flam’.
usage: The garden gnomes wearing tiny scarves were pure ___ on her part.

definitions.plain: A pleasant daydream; being lost in dreamy thought.
definitions.poetic: The little rowboat the mind takes out when nobody is asking it to steer.
definitions.riddle: Your eyes stay open while I carry you elsewhere; a dropped teacup calls you back.

etymology: From an old French word for wild rejoicing and rambling talk; crossing the Channel, it grew quiet and dreamy.
usage: The lecture dissolved into a ___ about lighthouses and summer storms.

definitions.plain: The earthy smell of rain falling on dry ground.
definitions.poetic: The ground’s held breath, released at the first kind touch of rain.
definitions.riddle: I am born when thirsty dust drinks; you smell me before you hear the storm.

etymology: Greek: stone joined with ichor, the golden blood of the gods — coined by two Australian scientists in 1964.
usage: After the drought broke, the whole street smelled of ___.

definitions.plain: Twilight; the fading light just after sunset.
definitions.poetic: The blue seam where day is stitched quietly into night.
definitions.riddle: Neither lamp nor dark, I am the hour when bats and porch lights wake together.

etymology: From Old English by way of Scots, kin to ‘glow’ — an hour kept alive in northern songs.
usage: Children were called in from the ___ one by one.

definitions.plain: Calm, peaceful, and golden — used of remembered happy times.
definitions.poetic: Weather borrowed from a kinder year, kept pressed between the mind’s pages.
definitions.riddle: I nest on a flat sea in midwinter and make the storms wait their turn.

etymology: From the Greek name for the kingfisher, which was said to nest on a becalmed sea.
usage: They spoke of the ___ summers before the mill closed.

definitions.plain: Sweet and smooth to hear, like a flowing voice or melody.
definitions.poetic: Speech that pours slow and amber, coating the ear like warm honey.
definitions.riddle: I describe the voice you would follow into a third hour of the story.

etymology: From the Latin for honey and for flowing — a compliment first paid to saints’ sermons.
usage: The announcer’s ___ baritone made even the shipping news soothing.

definitions.plain: The soft partial shadow around the edge of a full shadow.
definitions.poetic: The gray hem on night’s coat, where light and dark trade whispers.
definitions.riddle: In an eclipse I am the almost: not the bite of darkness, only its breath.

etymology: Coined by the astronomer Kepler from the Latin for ‘almost’ and ‘shadow’.
usage: The cat slept in the ___ of the lamplight, half gold, half gray.

definitions.plain: Nobly impractical; chasing ideals without regard for reality.
definitions.poetic: Armored in daydreams, riding out to rescue what never asked for saving.
definitions.riddle: I tilt at windmills and call them giants; sensible people sigh at me, and secretly cheer.

etymology: After the lean Spanish knight of a 1605 novel, who mistook windmills for giants and inns for castles.
usage: Restoring the ruined lighthouse by hand was a ___ project, and he began anyway.

definitions.plain: A soft whispering or rustling sound.
definitions.poetic: The hush the poplars pass along, leaf to leaf, like a secret.
definitions.riddle: I am what wind says in a library voice.

etymology: Latin, an imitative word — say it slowly and you hear the sound it names.
usage: A ___ of turning pages filled the reading room.

definitions.plain: Lasting only a very short time.
definitions.poetic: Beautiful the way frost-flowers are beautiful: gone by the time the kettle sings.
definitions.riddle: Mayflies, rainbows, and perfect snowballs all swear allegiance to me.

etymology: From the Greek for ‘lasting a day’, first said of fevers, then of mayflies, then of everything dear.
usage: Chalk art is ___ by nature; the afternoon rain took the whole mural.

definitions.plain: A manuscript page reused after the earlier writing was scraped away, with traces remaining.
definitions.poetic: A page that keeps its ghosts: old ink dreaming under the new.
definitions.riddle: Scrape me and rewrite me — still the first story rises through the second like a watermark.

etymology: From the Greek for ‘scraped again’: parchment was dear, so monks rubbed old ink away and wrote atop the shadow.
usage: The city is a ___, Roman stones showing through the medieval walls.

definitions.plain: A long, pointless, complicated procedure or ramble of talk.
definitions.poetic: A corridor of little doors between you and the one simple thing you came for.
definitions.riddle: Fill in form nine to request form twelve: I am the dance, not the destination.

etymology: From the ‘Ragman roll’, a long medieval parchment of names and seals that came to mean any tedious catalogue.
usage: Renewing the permit was a two-hour ___ of stamps and queues.

definitions.plain: The warmth of the sun in winter.
definitions.poetic: January’s small mercy: sunlight with its kettle just off the boil.
definitions.riddle: Find me on a freezing day, on the south wall, where the cat already sits.

etymology: From a Latin word for basking in sunshine; recorded once in 1656 and promptly mislaid by the language.
usage: They turned their chairs to the window to borrow a little ___.

definitions.plain: Foggy, misty, and gray, as winter weather.
definitions.poetic: Weather wearing wool: the world gone soft-edged and near-sighted.
definitions.riddle: On my kind of morning the lighthouse earns its keep and the hills go missing.

etymology: From the French for winter mist, tracing back to the Latin name for the year’s shortest day.
usage: The harbor lay ___ and still, the ferries sounding their horns blind.

definitions.plain: Glittering with gold or tinsel; showily sparkling.
definitions.poetic: Dressed in borrowed starlight and pleased about it.
definitions.riddle: I am the glitter of the stage crown — all flash and no jewels.

etymology: From a French verb imitating the chime of coins; English borrowed the shine in the 1590s.
usage: The theatre lobby was ___ with mirrors and gilt.

definitions.plain: A sleepwalker; one who walks about at night.
definitions.poetic: A dreamer whose dreams put on slippers and take the stairs.
definitions.riddle: I climb stairs I never remember and wake owning cold feet.

etymology: Latin night joined to walking — the politer cousin of ‘somnambulist’.
usage: The old innkeeper, a gentle ___, was found dusting shelves at three in the morning.

definitions.plain: A tiny trace or spark of something.
definitions.poetic: One firefly’s worth of light — and sometimes that is enough to navigate by.
definitions.riddle: Lawyers hunt me in evidence, prospectors in gravel: the least gleam that still counts.

etymology: Latin for a spark; the courtroom borrowed it for the faintest glimmer of proof.
usage: There was not a ___ of doubt in her voice.

definitions.plain: A small fib; pretentious nonsense.
definitions.poetic: A lie in its Sunday best, small enough to curtsy.
definitions.riddle: Not quite a lie, says the teller; quite a lie, says the listener. I am the size of the difference.

etymology: Origin uncertain, perhaps from an old word for dawdling — collected among eighteenth-century slang.
usage: His account of catching the pike grew a fresh ___ with every telling.

definitions.plain: The empty space left in a barrel or bottle that is not quite full.
definitions.poetic: The breath a bottle keeps for itself, between wine and cork.
definitions.riddle: The kinder the pour, the larger I grow — I am what the cask no longer holds.

etymology: From an Old French verb meaning to fill a cask up to the eye — the word came to name what filling leaves behind.
usage: The cellar-master tapped each cask, listening for its ___.

definitions.plain: Of, or happening in, the evening.
definitions.poetic: Belonging to the lamp-lighting hour, when moths take the day shift’s place.
definitions.riddle: Morning glories ignore me; jasmine and owls keep my calendar.

etymology: From the Latin name for the first star of dusk, which also lent its name to sung prayers at day’s end.
usage: The café kept ___ hours, opening as the streetlights warmed.

definitions.plain: Strange and marvelous; rarely seen.
definitions.poetic: So unfamiliar the eye must learn it twice.
definitions.riddle: I once described comets and camels to villagers who had seen neither.

etymology: Old English: ‘seldom’ joined with ‘known’ — what is met so rarely it stays wondrous.
usage: A ___ light hung above the marsh, and the whole village came out to look.

definitions.plain: The close of the day; the hour when dusk gathers.
definitions.poetic: The day folding its letter and sealing it with a first star.
definitions.riddle: I am the hour the plough stops and the lamp is lit; my name is the old way of saying dusk.

etymology: Old English: the day’s last hour joined with ‘tide’, back when ‘tide’ still meant time, as in Yuletide.
usage: At ___ the bells rang the fields home.

definitions.plain: Last night.
definitions.poetic: The night just past, still warm on the pillow of memory.
definitions.riddle: I am gone mere hours, yet the ballads mourn me like a lost year.

etymology: A Scots contraction of an older phrase for the night just gone — beloved of Burns and the border ballads.
usage: ___ the frost came early and silvered all the panes.

definitions.plain: The day after tomorrow.
definitions.poetic: Tomorrow’s quieter sister, standing two steps down the road.
definitions.riddle: Skip tomorrow once and you land on me.

etymology: Middle English, joining ‘beyond’ to ‘morrow’; German still keeps its twin alive.
usage: The mended clock will be ready ___, the tinker promised.

definitions.plain: The wishbone of a fowl.
definitions.poetic: The little forked bone that holds a wish until two hands set it free.
definitions.riddle: Two pull; one keeps the longer half and the promise inside it. What bone am I?

etymology: Named for the cheerful custom of two diners snapping the forked breast-bone to see whose wish would keep.
usage: The cousins dried the ___ on the sill for tomorrow’s tug.

definitions.plain: In a direction against the sun’s course; counterclockwise.
definitions.poetic: The wrong way round the church, where folktales keep their trouble.
definitions.riddle: Walk with me thrice round the well and the stories say you’ll wake the luck you shouldn’t.

etymology: From Middle Low German, ‘against the course’ — the opposite of walking sunwise.
usage: She stirred the pot ___ and her aunt clucked at the omen.
